Conversion Factors / Abbreviations and Symbols (page iv) — "Conversion Factors"

claims.claim: Temperature in this manual is reported in degrees Celsius and is converted to degrees Fahrenheit with the equation °F = 1.8(°C) + 32.
claims.quote:
Temperature is reported in degrees Celsius (°C), which can be converted to degrees
Fahrenheit (°F) by use of the following equation: °F = 1.8(°C) + 32

claims.claim: Specific conductance is reported in microsiemens per centimeter at 25 degrees Celsius (μS/cm at 25 °C), which ties every reported conductivity value to a reference temperature of 25 °C.
claims.quote:
Specific conductance is reported in microsiemens per centimeter at 25 degrees
Celsius (μS/cm at 25 °C).

claims.claim: In this manual Eh is defined as a measure of the oxidation-reduction potential of a solution.
claims.quote: Eh 	measure of the oxidation-reduction potential of a solution

claims.claim: pH is defined as the negative base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen ion activity and is unitless.
claims.quote: pH 	negative base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen ion activity (unitless)

claims.claim: Milligrams per liter (mg/L), the unit used for dissolved-oxygen concentration in this manual, is equivalent to parts per million (ppm).
claims.quote: mg/L 	milligrams per liter (equivalent to parts per million [ppm])

claims.claim: The conversion-factor table gives 1 gallon = 3.785 liters, 1 pound avoirdupois = 0.4536 kilogram, 1 liter = 0.2642 gallon, and 1 liter = 61.02 cubic inches.
claims.quote:
gallon (gal) 	3.785 	liter (L)
pound, avoirdupois (lb) 	0.4536 	kilogram (kg)

Section 1.1 Overview of Multiparameter Instruments and start of 2.0 Equipment and Supplies — "MULTIPARAMETER INSTRUMENT"

claims.claim: A multiparameter instrument is defined as an electronic instrument containing sensors, each specific to a given physical, chemical, or biological property, bundled in a single housing called a sonde.
claims.quote:
MULTIPARAMETER INSTRUMENT: An electronic
instrument that contains sensors (each specific to the
measurement of a given physical, chemical, or biological
property) that are bundled in a single housing

claims.claim: Multiparameter instruments make simultaneous readings of several field measurements and therefore determine field measurements in considerably less time than using multiple single-parameter instruments.
claims.quote:
field measurements can be determined in
considerably less time than that generally required when using
multiple single-parameter instruments

claims.claim: Chapter A6.8 addresses short-term or discrete-measurement use of portable multiparameter instruments; for long-term or continuous-monitor deployment the reader is referred to Wagner and others (2006).
claims.quote:
addresses the short-term or discrete-mea-
surement use of portable multiparameter instruments. Refer to
Wagner and others (2006) for information about long-term or
continuous-monitor deployment.

claims.claim: The instrument manufacturer is the primary source of information about maintenance and use of a specific instrument, and where NFM requirements and the manufacturer's instructions differ, the more stringent procedure typically should be used.
claims.quote:
The more stringent procedures typi-
cally should be used.

claims.claim: Multiparameter sonde housings are available in diameters from about 4 inches (10 centimeters) to less than 2 inches (5.1 centimeters), and small-diameter sondes usable for downhole measurements in wells may have more limited wiper and sensor capability because fewer sensor ports are available.
claims.quote:
diameters from about 4 inches (in.) (10 centimeters [cm]) to
less than 2 in. (5.1 cm)

claims.claim: Multiparameter sondes are suitable for use in water that is fresh, brackish, saline, or contaminated, and are available for discrete site-visit measurements or for deployment at a stream, lake, reservoir, or well.
claims.quote:
their sondes or bodies are suitable for use in water that is
fresh, brackish, saline, or contaminated

chunks.locator: Section 2.0 and table 6.8–1 (Advantages and limitations of multiparameter instruments for field use)

claims.claim: Multiparameter instruments may be operated by applications on tablets or cell phones using wireless communication protocols, and may be powered by internal batteries or through cables to external devices such as wireless communicators, hand-held displays, or laptop computers.
claims.quote:
Instruments may be
powered by their own internal batteries or through cables con-
nected to external devices

claims.claim: Because maintenance, calibration, and use procedures for multiparameter instruments can change as technology changes, users must stay current on how their instrument operates and is maintained.
claims.quote:
Users must stay current with respect
to how their instrument operates and is maintained.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–1 lists as a limitation that one system inside the sonde is responsible for recording all parameters, so a failure of that system causes the loss of all parameter values at once — temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, specific conductance, ORP, and turbidity together.
claims.quote:
One system (inside the sonde) is responsible for recording all
parameters, which would cause the loss of all parameter values
upon failure.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–1 states that backup field instruments, either single parameter or multiparameter, are recommended to prevent data loss.
claims.quote:
Backup field instruments (single parameter or multiparameter) are
recommended to prevent data loss.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–1 states that measurements made in situ are likely more representative than measurements made in samples removed from their source.
claims.quote:
Measurements made in situ are likely more representative than
measurements made in samples removed from their source.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–1 lists two further limitations of multiparameter instruments: purchase costs are higher than for single-parameter instruments, and calibration may require a greater volume of standards for rinsing.
claims.quote:
Calibration may require use of a greater volume of standards for
rinsing than that needed for single-parameter instruments.

Section 2.0 Equipment and Supplies and 2.1 Equipment Transport — "commonly bundled in sondes used for USGS"

claims.claim: Sensors for water temperature, specific electrical conductance, pH, dissolved-oxygen concentration, and turbidity are the ones commonly bundled together in sondes used for USGS water-quality studies.
claims.quote:
for the determination of water temperature, specific electrical
conductance (SC), pH, dissolved-oxygen (DO) concentration
and turbidity are commonly bundled in sondes used for USGS
water-quality

claims.claim: Permanent sensors for barometric pressure (for use with a DO sensor), water depth (vented or unvented), and location (GPS) are either standard equipment with many multiparameter instruments or can be added at extra cost, which ties dissolved-oxygen measurement to an onboard barometric-pressure sensor.
claims.quote:
Permanent sensors for measuring baro-
metric pressure (for use with a DO sensor), water depth (either
vented or unvented), and location (global positioning systems)

claims.claim: Oxidation-reduction potential (Eh) is a nonpermanent sensor that, along with fluorescence, velocity, nitrate, ammonia, ammonium, chloride, and chlorophyll sensors, can be added to many sondes through sensor ports rather than being standard.
claims.quote:
Nonpermanent
sensors for measuring oxidation-reduction potential (Eh), fluo-
rescence1, velocity, and concentrations of nitrate, ammonia,
ammonium, chloride, and chlorophyll can be added to

claims.claim: The number of sensors that can be bundled in a given sonde depends on the number of ports available in the instrument model, typically four to seven.
claims.quote:
number of ports available in an instrument model, typically
four to seven

claims.claim: When selecting a sensor, consult the manufacturer's recommendations and specifications while considering the environmental conditions to be encountered, the study's data-quality objectives, and the specific benefit of the sensor technology for the anticipated field conditions.
claims.quote:
taking into consideration the environmental conditions to be
encountered, the data-quality objectives of the study, and the
specific benefit of a particular sensor technology

claims.claim: Table 6.8–2 lists the equipment specifications required for field measurements with a multiparameter instrument and table 6.8–3 lists the required calibration-solution specifications, and the requirements in both tables may be modified to fit specific project needs.
claims.quote:
The requirements in tables 6.8–2 and 6.8–3 may be modified
to fit specific project needs.

claims.claim: Fluorescence sensors indicate different algal pigment concentrations, with additional information in NFM chapter A7.4 and Booth and others (2023).
claims.quote:
1Fluorescence sensors indicate different algal pigment concentrations; see
NFM chapter A7.4 and Booth and others (2023) for additional information.

claims.claim: For transportation and storage a padded case that protects the sonde from shock is required, the padding must be of a type that will not absorb water, and hard-sided cases should be equipped with a vent so internal pressure can equalize with the atmosphere.
claims.quote:
use a padded case that protects the sonde from
shock. The padding should be of a type that will not absorb
water. Hard-sided cases should be equipped with a vent so
that internal pressure can

claims.claim: Sondes should not be exposed to extreme heat or cold, and the transport case must not be exposed to direct sunlight in order to avoid solar heating of the equipment inside.
claims.quote:
Do not expose the case to direct sunlight in order to avoid
solar heating of the equipment inside.

claims.claim: Sensors can easily be damaged if handled improperly, and some sensors require storage and transportation in a wet or moist environment while others do not, so the manufacturer's recommendations must be checked.
claims.quote:
Some sensors require storage and transporta-
tion in a wet/moist environment, whereas others do not,
check the manufacturer’s recommendations.

chunks.locator: Table 6.8–2. Specifications for multiparameter instruments — "Sensor1 	Specifications"

claims.claim: Table 6.8–2 requires a pH sensor with a range of at least 2 to 12 (preferably 0 to 14) pH units, accuracy of ±0.1 pH units, and resolution of ±0.01 pH units.
claims.quote: pH and millivolt 	Range of at least 2 to 12, preferably 0 to 14, pH units. Accuracy, ±0.1 pH units. Resolution, ±0.01 pH units.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–2 requires the millivolt readout of the pH/millivolt sensor to have an accuracy of ±0.1 mV.
claims.quote: Millivolt readout—accuracy, ±0.1 mV.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–2 requires a temperature sensor with a range of at least –5 to +45 °C and an accuracy of ±0.2 °C.
claims.quote: Temperature 	Range, of at least –5 to +45 °C. Accuracy, ±0.2 °C.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–2 requires specific electrical conductance accuracy of the greater of ±5 percent of reading or ±2 μS/cm.
claims.quote: SC 	Accuracy, the greater of ±5 percent of reading or ±2 μS/cm.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–2 requires an optical (luminescent-sensor method) dissolved-oxygen sensor with a range of 0.01 to 20 mg/L and accuracy of ±0.1 mg/L.
claims.quote: DO 	Optical sensor (luminescent-sensor method)—range 0.01 to 20 mg/L. Accuracy, ±0.1 mg/L.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–2 states that turbidity range and accuracy depend on the instrument type, manufacturer, and field conditions rather than being fixed, and refers the reader to NFM A6.7.
claims.quote: Turbidity 	Range and accuracy depend on the instrument type, manufacturer, and field conditions (see NFM A6.7).

claims.claim: Most multiparameter-instrument turbidity sensors use a monochrome light source with spectral output typically near infrared (780–900 nm), typically a light-emitting diode, and one detector at 90-degree orientation to the light source.
claims.quote:
monochrome light source with a spectral output typically near infrared (780–900 nm), typically a light-
emitting diode, and one detector at 90-degree orientation to the light source.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–2 requires ORP accuracy of ±5 mV and refers the reader to NFM A6.5 and the manufacturer's instructions for Eh measurements using the platinum electrode.
claims.quote: ORP 	Accuracy, ±5 mV. For guidance on Eh measurements using the platinum electrode, refer to NFM A6.5 and

claims.claim: Table 6.8–2 requires selecting instruments that incorporate an altimeter/barometer measuring air pressure to at least the nearest 1 mm Hg, the barometric input a dissolved-oxygen sensor depends on.
claims.quote: Air pressure 	Select instruments that incorporate an altimeter/barometer that measures to at least the nearest 1 mm Hg.

claims.claim: The sensor list in table 6.8–2 is to be modified to meet the specific needs of the field effort.
claims.quote: 1 Modify this list to meet the specific needs of the field effort

Table 6.8–4 (Ancillary supplies) and start of table 6.8–3 (Specifications for calibration solutions)

claims.claim: Table 6.8–4 specifies a standard flow-through cell/chamber obtained from the instrument manufacturer, commonly used for groundwater or other water pumped from the source into the airtight cell for measurement.
claims.quote: Standard flow-through cell/chamber, obtained from the manufacturer of the instrument.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–4 requires the calibration thermometer and barometer to be NIST-certified or NIST-traceable, which governs both the temperature calibration and the barometric pressure used for dissolved-oxygen calibration (see NFM A6.1 and A6.2).
claims.quote: Calibration thermometer and barometer 	NIST-certified or NIST-traceable. (see NFM A6.1 and A6.2 for USGS standard

claims.claim: Table 6.8–4 specifies a protective, insulated, vented carrying case that is white or another reflective color for transport and storage.
claims.quote: Carrying case 	Protective, insulated, case, vented, white or other reflective color, for transport and storage.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–4 requires one logbook per instrument or interchangeable sensor for recording calibrations, maintenance, and repairs, travelling with the instrument or sensor or being digitally accessible.
claims.quote:
One per instrument or interchangeable sensor, for recording calibrations, maintenance, and
repairs.

claims.claim: Deionized water used for rinsing sensors must have a maximum conductivity of 1 μS/cm (ASTM Type 2) and be dispensed from a plastic bottle.
claims.quote:
Maximum conductivity of 1 μS/cm (ASTM Type 2) for rinsing sensors, dispensed from a
plastic bottle.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–4 specifies laboratory-grade lint-free paper tissues (for example Kimwipes) and cloth or paper towels for DO sensor calibration and checks and general cleanup.
claims.quote: Towels, cloth or paper 	For DO sensor calibration and checks, and general cleanup.

claims.claim: Cleaning brushes should be of various sizes but generally small and soft to prevent scratching the sensors or other surfaces.
claims.quote:
Brushes of various sizes, but generally small and soft to prevent scratching the sensor(s) or
other surfaces.

claims.claim: Waste-disposal containers must be appropriate for safe containment of regulated substances and dedicated to their respective waste material, with ZoBell's solution, acid, and turbidity calibration solutions given as examples.
claims.quote:
respective waste material (examples: ZoBell’s solution, acid, and turbidity calibration
solutions).

claims.claim: For all sensor-calibration solutions, the respective Safety Data Sheet must be kept on hand in the laboratory and in the field, and waste disposed of according to local regulations using a licensed disposal company if necessary.
claims.quote:
Keep the respective SDS guidance on hand in the laboratory and in the field. Dispose of waste
according to local regulations, using a licensed disposal company, if necessary.

claims.claim: The standard pH buffers are pH 4, 7, and 10, and temperature-correction charts supplied by the buffer manufacturer or distributor are required, tying pH calibration to the buffer temperature (see NFM A6.4).
claims.quote:
Standard buffers are pH 4, 7, and 10. Temperature-correction chart(s) supplied by the buffer
manufacturer or distributor are required.

claims.claim: Specific-conductance standards must be chosen nearest to and/or bracketing the expected measurement or range, with additional bracketing standards selected to field check the calibration (see NFM A6.3).
claims.quote:
Choose the SC standard(s) nearest to and/or that bracket(s) the expected measurement or range. To
field check the calibration, select additional standard(s) that bracket the expected sample SC.

claims.claim: Table 6.8–4 requires checking that batteries are fully charged and bringing spares, and specifies disposable nonpowdered nitrile gloves available from USGS One-Stop Shopping.
claims.quote: Batteries and (or) battery pack(s) 	Check that batteries are fully charged; bring spares.

chunks.locator: Table 6.8–3. Specifications for calibration solutions — "DO standard 	Zero-DO solution"

claims.claim: The DO standard is a zero-DO solution made by dissolving 2 grams of sodium sulfite in 1 liter of deionized water, prepared onsite or during the week of use, and it can also be obtained commercially (see NFM A6.2).
claims.quote:
Zero-DO solution. Dissolve 2 g of sodium sulfite in 1 L of DIW (prepared onsite or during the week of
use).

claims.claim: The ORP standard is ZoBell's solution, which contains cyanide and may be harmful if absorbed through skin, inhaled, or swallowed, so the Safety Data Sheet must be checked for safe handling (see NFM A6.5).
claims.quote:
ZoBell’s solution. This solution contains cyanide and may be harmful if absorbed through skin,
inhaled, or swallowed.

claims.claim: Most turbidity sensor manufacturers recommend either formazin-based or SDVB-polymer standards for calibration, and gel or solid verification standards must not be used for calibrating instruments (see NFM A6.7).
claims.quote:
Most sensor manufacturers recommend either formazin-based or SDVB-
polymer standards for calibration. Do not use gel or solid verification standards for calibrating
instruments.

claims.claim: Turbidity-free water is deionized water filtered through a membrane filter of 0.2 micrometer or smaller pore size.
claims.quote: Turbidity-free water which is DIW filtered through a ≤0.2-μm membrane filter.

Section 2.2 Instrument Maintenance and Storage — "Each instrument requires a dedicated logbook"

claims.claim: A separate logbook recording instrument repair, maintenance, and calibration history is required to be maintained for each field instrument or replaceable sensor that stores calibration information in the sensor's internal processor.
claims.quote:
A separate logbook in which instrument repair, mainte-
nance, and calibration history information is recorded
is required to be maintained for each field instrument
or replaceable sensor

claims.claim: Pages of a paper instrument logbook should be prenumbered consecutively and must not be skipped or torn out, water-resistant paper is recommended, and paper logbooks are available to USGS personnel through One-Stop shopping as item Q609FLD.
claims.quote:
The pages of a paper instru-
ment logbook should be prenumbered consecutively.
Do not skip or tear out pages. Water-resistant paper
is recommended.

claims.claim: Office of Water Quality Technical Memorandum 2016.09 recommends that all water-quality records, including logbooks, be collected electronically wherever feasible and specifies requirements for electronic records.
claims.quote:
Technical Memorandum 2016.09 recommends that all
water-quality records, including logbooks, be collected
electronically wherever feasible

claims.claim: Blue or black indelible ballpoint pen must be used on paper forms and in logbooks; pencil is not acceptable and felt-tipped pens such as Sharpie markers should not be used because they could compromise data quality for samples collected for volatile organic compound analysis.
claims.quote:
Use of a pencil is
not acceptable; felt-tipped pens (for example, Sharpie
markers) should not be used

claims.claim: Instruments must not be left in vehicles during temperature extremes, and it is good practice to transport and store them in an insulated case or cooler.
claims.quote:
Do not leave instruments in vehicles during extremes
in temperature.

claims.claim: Cable connection and sensor O-rings must be inspected and cleaned annually at a minimum, lubricated lightly with silicone grease or Krytox, and any damaged ones replaced.
claims.quote:
Inspect and clean the cable connection and sensor
O-rings annually, at a minimum. Lubricate them
lightly with silicone grease or Krytox.

claims.claim: Cables must be stored clean, dry, and neatly coiled in coils no tighter than 6 inches in diameter, with protective plugs used on connectors when not in use.
claims.quote:
clean, dry, and neatly coiled (no tighter than 6-in-
diameter coils)

claims.claim: Instrument software and firmware must be kept up to date, with a check for manufacturer updates every 6 months at a minimum, following the manufacturer's installation instructions.
claims.quote:
Check for updates from
the manufacturer every 6 months at a minimum and
follow the manufacturer’s installation instructions.

claims.claim: Sensors must be rinsed with deionized water immediately after each use.
claims.quote:
Rinse the sensors immediately after each use with
deionized water (DIW).

claims.claim: A dirty sonde body or hand-held display (not the sensors themselves) is cleaned with a mild, nonphosphate detergent solution using a small nonabrasive brush, cotton swab, or cloth, followed by a thorough water rinse.
claims.quote:
clean it with a mild, nonphosphate detergent solution
by using a small, nonabrasive brush or cotton swab
or cloth, and follow with a thorough water rinse.

claims.claim: Cables must be routinely inspected for damage and electronic connectors and sensor ports inspected for corrosion.
claims.quote:
Routinely inspect cables for damage, and electronic
connectors and sensor ports for corrosion.

claims.claim: The maintenance recommendations in section 2.2 pertain to instruments used over discrete or short attended intervals; for long-term or unattended deployment the reader is referred to Wagner and others (2006) and the manufacturer's instructions.
claims.quote:
For maintenance of instruments
intended for long-term or unattended instrument deployment,
refer to Wagner and others (2006)

chunks.locator: Section 2.2, sensor/sonde care and wiper maintenance bullets — "Wiper and wiper-brush maintenance"

claims.claim: Organic solvents and other corrosive solutions must be avoided for cleaning sensors unless indicated in guidance given by the manufacturer.
claims.quote:
Avoid using organic solvents or other corrosive solu-
tions to clean the sensors unless indicated in guid-

claims.claim: The sonde and sensors must not be coated with protective or anti-fouling paint except as specifically instructed by the manufacturer.
claims.quote:
Do not coat the sonde or sensors with protective or
anti-fouling paint, except as specifically instructed
by the manufacturer.

claims.claim: The wiper pad and wiper brush must be inspected for dirt, deterioration, and damage after each use of the instrument, noting that not all instruments have a wiper or wiper-brush mechanism.
claims.quote:
Inspect the wiper pad and (or) wiper brush for dirt,
deterioration, and damage after each use of the
instrument.

claims.claim: Wiper pads must be checked for wear, excessive discoloration, and particle accumulation and changed as needed, and the wiper arm must be checked to confirm it is parking properly.
claims.quote:
Check wiper pads for wear, excessive discoloration,
and particle accumulation, and change the pads
as needed. Check that the wiper arm is parking
properly.

claims.claim: Wiper-brush bristles can be cleaned with warm soapy water and a soft toothbrush followed by a deionized-water rinse, and the wiper brush is replaced or reconditioned when it shows excessive splaying.
claims.quote:
Warm soapy water and a soft toothbrush can be used
to clean wiper-brush bristles. Rinse with DIW.

claims.claim: For short-term storage some sensors need a small amount of storage solution added to the protective (transport) cap or calibration cup, per the manufacturer's instructions.
claims.quote:
For short-term storage, some sensors need a small
amount of the storage solution added to the protec-
tive (transport) cap or calibration cup

claims.claim: Manufacturers may have instructions specific to their sensors, so the manufacturer's operating manual must be checked for each instrument in use.
claims.quote:
Manufacturers may have instructions specific to their
sensors—check the manufacturer’s operating manual
for each instrument that will be in use.

chunks.locator: Overlap-only chunk repeating the wiper-brush and short-term storage bullets — "Replace or recondition the wiper brush"
Section 2.2 storage bullets and section 3.0 Calibration — "The following order is recommended for performing parameter calibrations"

claims.claim: For long-term storage, defined as longer than 1 week, the internal batteries are removed, after checking the instrument manual for guidance before removing them.
claims.quote:
For long-term storage (longer than 1 week), remove
the internal batteries

claims.claim: Multiparameter instruments are stored in a carrying case or plastic container with closed-cell nonabsorbent foam cushion for shock protection, kept out of direct sunlight and protected against extremely hot or cold temperatures.
claims.quote:
Store multiparameter instruments in a carrying case
or plastic container with closed-cell (nonabsorbent)
foam cushion (for shock protection).

claims.claim: Sensors not routinely collecting data can be removed from the sonde for safe storage, but the temperature sensor should not be removed, and empty sensor ports must be sealed with an appropriate plug with all electrical connections clean, dry, waterproof, and protected from dust.
claims.quote:
The tem-
perature sensor should not be removed.

claims.claim: Multiparameter instruments are required to be tested and their sensors calibrated or checked before each field use, which applies to the temperature, specific conductance, pH, dissolved oxygen, ORP, and turbidity sensors alike.
claims.quote:
Multiparameter instruments are required to be tested
and the sensors calibrated or checked before each field
use.

claims.claim: Calibrations are preferably done under laboratory or indoor conditions and then checked and verified in the field; if laboratory or indoor conditions are not available, instruments may be calibrated in the field.
claims.quote:
Preferably, calibrations are done under laboratory or
indoor conditions and are checked and verified in the field.

claims.claim: NFM chapters A6.1 through A6.7 are the definitive information for calibration of instruments and are not replaced by the general guidance in chapter A6.8 or by guidance in previous versions of that chapter.
claims.quote:

gaps: No ecological or health interpretation of any value — zero occurrences of "healthy", "aquatic life", or "hypoxia". Like every USGS chapter in this corpus it says how to obtain a defensible number, never what the number means.
No full calibration procedure per metric. Buffers and Zobell solution are mentioned in passing but the methods live in A6.1-A6.7; an operator cannot calibrate a probe from this chapter alone.
No sensor replacement or end-of-life guidance — zero occurrences of "replacement". Table 6.8-6 troubleshoots unstable readings but never says when a sensor is finished.
No sample holding times or preservation guidance — zero occurrences of "holding time".

Salinity appears only three times and barometric pressure once, so DO salinity and barometric correction — which A6.2 treats at length with tables — is not settled here despite this being the multiparameter-sonde chapter.

No turbidity unit-conversion guidance. FNU appears three times and NTU once, with no statement of how or whether values from differing optical designs can be compared. A6.7 is the only source for that.
No guidance on instrument cost, procurement, or model selection beyond generic sensor categories, so "which sonde should we buy" is unanswerable.
No unattended long-term deployment protocol: the chapter is written around discrete field visits and purging, not continuous monitoring.
summary.notes: COMPLETE — all 34 chunks extracted. CROSS-DOCUMENT FINDING: Table 6.8-5 here and Table 6.0-1 in NFM A6.0 state the SAME stabilization criteria numerically — temperature ±0.2 °C, specific conductance ±5 μS/cm at or below 100 μS/cm and ±3 percent above, dissolved oxygen ±0.2 mg/L, pH ±0.1 unit, turbidity ±0.5 turbidity units or 5 percent whichever is greater. The two chapters agree; this is redundancy across documents, NOT a precedence conflict. A cross-document fixture can legitimately require both sources, but a fixture premised on them disagreeing would be false. The 60-second minimum thermal-equilibrium wait at each new depth is stated for both surface water and groundwater, with the note that some instruments need longer and manufacturer guidance governs.
